Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette: Darius, a twenty-seven-year-old of African heritage, was eleven when the incidents stopped being rare and became a rhythm his body memorized. He remembered the particular scratch of his caregiver's heavy cotton cardigan against his collarbone, a specific, gritty texture that caught every time the older man's hands closed around his shoulders. That same fabric was always paired with a sharp, damp warmth pressing against his skin, the kind that settled in when the kitchen window cracked open to let in the humid air. He did not simply feel pressure; he felt that exact temperature shift and that particular weave against his neck, a tactile warning that a strike was coming. Years later, a PCL-5 score of 56 tracks closely with his daily experience, but the numbers only partially capture how he carries that memory in his shoulders. When the air conditioning kicks on, sending a cool, damp draft across his right arm, his muscles tense. When the taxi's worn upholstery scrapes against his thigh, he goes still, certain the weight is about to turn into a grip. The steering wheel has become both his anchor and his watchtower. Darius drives with a quiet, constant alertness, his shoulders set high, his gaze sweeping the sidewalks and the cars that pull alongside him. He cannot quite accept that a calm street means safety; even when the sun is bright and the passengers speak in steady tones, he finds it impossible to believe that the danger has truly passed. He hears footsteps behind him on the curb and matches their pace, his body bracing before he registers that the stranger is walking away. This watchfulness sits beside his tendency to take risks. He sometimes runs yellow lights or cuts across lanes without signaling, as if testing whether the road will still hold him if he pushes. He drives late shifts more often than he used to. He has learned to avoid intimacy by keeping relationships light and transactional. He prefers the predictable rhythm of fares and receipts to the expectations of closeness. When a passenger leans forward to ask a personal question, he answers with a nod and a glance at the road. He redirects his attention to the meter or the steady hum of the engine. He fills the cabin with low-volume radio static or adjusts his sunglasses until the visual field narrows just enough. He began taking his drugs in the evenings. The warmth settled over his chest. The noise quieted. Over time, Darius has felt permanently changed, as if the boy he was is still somewhere behind him, and the man he has become is built from watchfulness. Even when he sits still in his apartment, his chest tightens and his hands twitch, as if he is still bracing against a blow that never quite lands. His body keeps reacting as though the danger is still near, independent of the quiet hours and the empty streets. He has lost his connection to his community and culture, not through a single rupture, but through a slow fading of shared rituals and familiar voices. The taxi's upholstery, the temperature of the cab, the sound of heels clicking on wet pavement-these are no longer just background details. They are reminders. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single breakdown, but a Tuesday afternoon when a passenger's hand brushed his arm, and the specific texture of the man's cotton sleeve made his heart hammer against his ribs. He found himself pulling away, unable to trust the gentle touch, unable to quiet the alertness in his own chest. He is here now, hoping to understand why his body sounds the alarm so easily, and wondering if he can finally let the safety in.
